notes:
Task and constraints: Enumerate every path in a directed acyclic graph from node 0 to the final node.
Idea: Use depth-first search, extending a mutable path along each outgoing edge and backtracking after recursion.
Technique and why it applies: Each branch explores one next node. When the path reaches the final node, a copy is appended to results so later backtracking does not mutate the stored path.
Invariant: step is the current path from source to the active node.
Edge cases: The code assumes graph is nonempty and acyclic. It passes graph[0] as the first candidate list and uses step[-1] to identify the current node.
Complexity: The search visits path prefixes and outputs every path; time is proportional to total path length and can be exponential, with O(V) recursion/path space aside from output.

Task and constraints: Return all paths from node 0 to node n-1 in a DAG.
Idea: Recursively visit each outgoing neighbor while maintaining the current path.
Technique and why it applies: DFS explores every possible branch. When the destination is reached, path[:] stores an independent copy; popping after recursion restores the parent path.
Invariant: path contains the sequence of vertices from source to the current vertex.
Edge cases: A graph with one node returns [[0]]. The algorithm relies on the graph being acyclic, as the code does not maintain a visited set.
Complexity: Work is proportional to the number of paths times their average length and may be exponential; active path and recursion use O(V) space beyond output.

Task and constraints: Find the rotation index of nums that maximizes the score, where a value scores when it is no greater than its rotated index.
Idea: Track values that remain qualified as the rotation increases, using a heap of index-minus-value thresholds.
Technique and why it applies: target increments each rotation; values whose threshold is below it are removed, and the value crossing the end is reinserted with its wrapped threshold. Heap size represents the score.
Invariant: qualified contains threshold values that qualify for the current rotation.
Edge cases: heappush and heappop are used without importing heapq, so the snippet needs those names defined externally. Empty nums returns zero by default.
Complexity: Each value is inserted and removed at most once, giving O(n log n) time and O(n) heap space.

Task and constraints: Return the smallest rotation index that achieves the highest score.
Idea: Use a difference array to record where each element stops scoring as the array is rotated.
Technique and why it applies: Each element contributes a score across a range of rotations; decrementing change at its loss boundary and prefix-summing computes the score for every rotation. index(max(change)) selects the earliest maximum.
Invariant: After prefix accumulation, change[k] is the score adjustment for rotation k, up to a shared baseline.
Edge cases: The method assumes nums is nonempty; otherwise max on an empty list fails. The first maximum index implements the smallest-index tie break.
Complexity: Building and prefix-summing change take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Compute how much champagne remains in a specified glass after pouring into the top of a tower.
Idea: Simulate overflow row by row, splitting excess equally between the two glasses below.
Technique and why it applies: A glass retains at most one unit; quantity stores the amount reaching each coordinate. Only positive overflow is propagated to the next row.
Invariant: quantity[(i,j)] is the amount arriving at glass (i,j) before its excess is sent downward.
Edge cases: defaultdict is used but not imported in the snippet. If no glass overflows in a row, flag remains false and the loop stops early.
Complexity: Processing rows through r visits O(r²) glasses and uses O(r²) dictionary space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum swaps needed to make both sequences strictly increasing at every index.
Idea: Recursively choose whether to keep or swap the current pair, memoizing the minimum future swaps by index and previous swap state.
Technique and why it applies: Each action is permitted only when both resulting sequences exceed the previous values. The recurrence adds one for a swap and takes the minimum legal option.
Invariant: solve returns the minimum swaps from index i onward given prev1, prev2, and whether the preceding position was swapped.
Edge cases: The memo table is keyed only by i and swaped, but the previous values also depend on the prior decision; that is sufficient for this fixed input and state encoding. The initial previous values of -1 assume input values are nonnegative.
Complexity: There are O(n) memo slots with constant transitions, so O(n) time and space.

Task and constraints: Minimize swaps between corresponding elements of two arrays so both arrays become strictly increasing.
Idea: Maintain rolling DP costs for the current index with and without swapping that position.
Technique and why it applies: If both arrays increase without crossing, prior no-swap leads to no-swap and prior swap leads to swap. If cross comparisons hold, the previous swap state can transition to the opposite current state.
Invariant: dp_no_swap and dp_swap store the minimum swap counts for the latest processed index under each current choice.
Edge cases: The code assumes arrays are nonempty; len(A)=0 would index an invalid slot. It uses two alternating slots to reduce memory.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find all eventual safe nodes in a directed graph, meaning every path from the node eventually terminates.
Idea: Start with terminal nodes and recursively test other nodes for cycles, treating known safe nodes as successful branches.
Technique and why it applies: The loops list tracks the current DFS path; revisiting a node on that path detects a cycle. A node is added to ans only if every reachable branch succeeds.
Invariant: loops contains the active recursion path, and ans contains terminal or previously confirmed safe nodes.
Edge cases: Membership checks in lists and loops are linear, and the algorithm can repeat large portions of the graph. The recursion can also hit Python's recursion limit on deep graphs.
Complexity: Worst-case time can be O(V(V+E)) or worse due to repeated DFS and list membership, with O(V) active path storage.

Task and constraints: Return the number of bricks that fall after each hit, excluding the brick directly hit.
Idea: Remove all hit bricks, build connected components with a disjoint-set structure, then restore hits in reverse and measure roof connectivity growth.
Technique and why it applies: A virtual roof node joins all stable top-row bricks. When reversing a hit, any increase in the roof component size minus the restored brick counts newly stabilized bricks.
Invariant: parent and sz represent connected brick components, including the virtual roof; res stores the reverse-time connectivity gain for each hit.
Edge cases: The empty set records hits on originally empty cells so they are not restored. The grid is modified in place. The snippet uses defaultdict() without a factory for parent, but each key is initialized before find calls.
Complexity: With R*C cells and H hits, union-find work is near O(RC+H) times inverse-Ackermann factors, and storage is O(RC).

Task and constraints: Count distinct Morse-code transformations among the given lowercase words.
Idea: Translate each word character-by-character and count unique encoded strings.
Technique and why it applies: The mapping assigns each letter a Morse code, and dictionary keys deduplicate words that have identical transformations.
Invariant: cnt contains one key for each distinct transformation encountered.
Edge cases: Empty words encode as the empty string and are counted once. The dictionary counter values are unnecessary; duplicate transformations only need not create new keys.
Complexity: Runtime is O(total characters) plus string concatenation costs, and space is O(total encoded output) across distinct transformations.

Task and constraints: Count the distinct Morse-code strings produced by the input words.
Idea: Build each word's Morse representation and insert it into a set.
Technique and why it applies: Set uniqueness removes duplicate representations automatically, so the answer is the set size.
Invariant: lookup contains every distinct encoding processed so far.
Edge cases: An empty input list returns zero. The code assumes words contain lowercase English letters.
Complexity: Encoding takes O(total input characters) expected time, with space proportional to the stored encoded strings.

Task and constraints: Determine whether an array can be split into two nonempty parts with equal average.
Idea: Use sets of reachable sums for each subset size up to half the array length.
Technique and why it applies: Adding each number updates sums for one more selected item, and reverse size iteration prevents reusing that item in the same iteration. A subset of size k has the same average when its sum equals total_sum*k/n.
Invariant: DP[k] contains sums achievable by selecting exactly k processed elements.
Edge cases: A.sort() mutates the input but is not needed for the set DP. The code tests a floating-point quotient for membership, which can be inaccurate; integer divisibility and integer sums are safer.
Complexity: The number of reachable sums can grow exponentially, so worst-case time and space are exponential despite the bounded subset-size dimension.

Task and constraints: Check whether a nonempty subset has the same average as the whole array.
Idea: First rule out impossible subset sizes using divisibility, then track subset sums by subset cardinality.
Technique and why it applies: A size-i subset must sum to s*i/n, which is possible only if s*i is divisible by n. The DP sets record sums achievable with each size.
Invariant: sums[i] contains sums formed by selecting i elements from the processed prefix.
Edge cases: The helper call possible(n, s) checks whether any size through n//2 can have an integer target sum. Empty input is not handled explicitly and would divide by zero.
Complexity: Reachable subset sums can be exponential in n; the sets use exponential worst-case space, with a polynomial number of cardinality layers.

Task and constraints: Return the number of lines and the width used on the last line when writing s with given lowercase letter widths and a 100-unit line limit.
Idea: Add each character's width to the current line and start a new line if the total exceeds 100.
Technique and why it applies: The current character is placed at the beginning of the new line after overflow, so px resets to that character's width.
Invariant: l is the current line number and px is the width occupied on that line.
Edge cases: The code prints each character's code point, an unwanted debugging side effect. If a single width exceeded 100, it would still place that character on a line, though constraints normally prevent this.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine how many lines are needed for a string and the width of the final line, with a maximum width of 100.
Idea: Accumulate each character's width and move to a new line when the current width exceeds 100.
Technique and why it applies: The character that causes overflow is placed on the next line, so the line count increases and the current width becomes that character's width.
Invariant: result[0] stores line count, while result[1] stores the current line's used width.
Edge cases: Empty S returns [1,0], matching the code's initial state. Letter widths are looked up by lowercase ASCII index.
Complexity: The string is scanned once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Maximize building heights while preserving the city's row and column skyline profiles.
Idea: Compute each row maximum and column maximum, then add each cell's allowed increase.
Technique and why it applies: A cell cannot exceed either skyline, so its final height is min(row_max, col_max). The difference between that bound and its original height is the increase.
Invariant: mxr and mxc store the original skyline heights for each row and column.
Edge cases: The inner summation loops over len(grid) for columns rather than len(grid[0]); this assumes a square grid, as in the standard problem. Empty grids would fail during indexing.
Complexity: Skyline computation and summation take O(N²) time and O(N) auxiliary space for an N-by-N grid.

Task and constraints: Find the total possible increase in city building heights without changing any row or column skyline.
Idea: Compute row and column maxima and sum the difference between each height and the smaller of those maxima.
Technique and why it applies: The skyline limits a cell to min(row maximum, column maximum); increasing each cell to that limit preserves both profiles.
Invariant: row_maxes and col_maxes hold the maximum of every original row and column.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty rectangular grid. itertools is imported but unused.
Complexity: The row/column maxima and cell sum take O(RC) time and O(R+C) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Compute the probability that soup A empties first, with half credit if both soups empty in the same serving.
Idea: Scale n into 25-ml units and memoize the probability for remaining amounts of both soups.
Technique and why it applies: Each serving operation has probability 1/4 and removes a fixed pair of amounts. The recurrence averages the four successor probabilities; boundary cases resolve when one or both soups are empty.
Invariant: dp(i,j) is the probability A empties first from the state with i and j units remaining.
Edge cases: For large n, the implementation returns 1.0 as an approximation justified by the problem's tolerance. The memo is local to the call.
Complexity: There are O(n²) scaled states and constant work per state, giving O(n²) time and space in scaled units.

Task and constraints: Estimate the probability that soup A empties first under four equally likely serving operations.
Idea: Use memoized recursion over scaled remaining soup amounts, with explicit terminal probabilities.
Technique and why it applies: The four operations each occur with probability 0.25, so their recursive probabilities are averaged. The state is scaled by 25 to match serving sizes.
Invariant: lookup[(a,b)] stores the probability from remaining scaled amounts a and b.
Edge cases: For N>=4800, the method returns 1.0 instead of computing the recurrence, relying on the probability being sufficiently close to one. Both-empty returns 0.5.
Complexity: The memoized recurrence has O((N/25)²) states and O(1) work per state, so O((N/25)²) time and space below the cutoff.

Task and constraints: Count words that can be stretched to match s by expanding runs of repeated characters of length at least three.
Idea: Compress each string into its sequence of run characters and run lengths, then compare corresponding runs.
Technique and why it applies: The character sequences must match; a candidate run cannot be longer than s's run, and if lengths differ, s's run must be at least three. The code decrements the count for any word violating those conditions.
Invariant: s_split and s_array describe target run characters and lengths; each candidate is checked run by run.
Edge cases: The empty-input branches return booleans rather than integer counts. The condition (num_s != num_word and num_s < 3) or (num_word > num_s) relies on operator precedence.
Complexity: Compression and comparison take O(total input characters) time, with O(n) temporary run arrays.
